nameStory: The word 'cattle' comes from the Old French 'chatel,' meaning property or wealth, which also gave us the word 'chattel.' For thousands of years, owning cattle was a sign of prosperity and status. Bulls and cows were so valuable that many ancient cultures used them as currency before coins were invented!
description: Domestic cattle are large, heavy-bodied farm animals that you'll recognize instantly by their distinctive 'moo' and gentle grazing behavior. These impressive mammals can weigh anywhere from 600 to over 2,000 pounds depending on the breed and sex. They have sturdy, rectangular bodies with four-chambered stomachs for digesting grass, short legs that end in split hooves, and most have prominent udders (females) or muscular necks (males). Their coats come in many colors and patterns, from solid black or brown to spotted or patched.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Unmistakably large and bulky with a rectangular body profile, standing 4-6 feet tall at the shoulder. Their massive, barrel-shaped torso sits on relatively short, thick legs ending in distinctive cloven hooves that leave heart-shaped tracks in mud.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Spend most of their time slowly grazing with heads down, moving in a calm, deliberate manner. They gather in groups and make distinctive 'mooing' vocalizations that can carry across fields. Watch for their methodical chewing motion even when resting.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Short, coarse hair that feels rough to the touch, coming in solid colors (black, brown, white) or patterns like patches and spots. Their coat may look sleek in summer but becomes shaggier and thicker in winter months.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Large, split-hoof prints that look like two curved crescents forming a heart shape, typically 4-5 inches long. In soft ground, you'll see deep impressions due to their substantial weight, often in well-worn paths to water or shelter.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Large, round, flat 'cow pies' of dung scattered throughout pastures with a distinctive barnyard smell. Look for well-worn trails through grass, rubbing marks on fence posts and trees where they scratch, and areas of closely cropped vegetation.

habitat: You'll find cattle in managed pastures, hayfields, and farm properties throughout New England's rural areas and suburbs. They prefer open grasslands with access to fresh water sources like ponds, streams, or water troughs. Most are contained within fenced areas, though some graze on hillside pastures with spectacular valley views.

seasonality.spring: Cattle are turned out to fresh green pastures, and you'll often see newborn calves staying close to their mothers. Their winter coats begin shedding, giving them a somewhat patchy appearance.
seasonality.summer: Most active during cooler morning and evening hours, seeking shade during hot afternoons. Their coats are at their shortest and sleekest, and you'll see them grazing continuously on lush grass.
seasonality.fall: Cattle may be moved to different pastures or brought closer to barns as grass growth slows. Their coats begin thickening for winter, and some herds are gathered for breeding season.
seasonality.winter: Develop thick, shaggy coats that may look almost fuzzy from a distance. Often kept closer to barns with supplemental hay feeding, and you'll see their breath steaming in cold air.

funFact: Cattle have an incredible sense of smell that's about 1,000 times stronger than humans — they can detect odors from up to 6 miles away and recognize individual people by scent alone!
confusionNotes: At a distance, cattle might be confused with horses, but cattle are much bulkier, move more slowly, and have the distinctive split hooves rather than single hooves. Remember: cattle 'moo,' horses 'neigh,' and cattle spend much more time with their heads down grazing.
contextualKnowledge: While we call them 'cows,' technically only adult females are cows — males are bulls and young ones are calves. Many people use 'cow' for all cattle, which is perfectly acceptable in casual conversation. These domestic animals descended from wild aurochs that went extinct in the 1600s.
compareHints: Domestic cattle are the only members of the genus Bos you'll encounter in New England, but they're related to bison (much more massive with shaggy heads and humped shoulders) and water buffalo (not found in our region). Unlike their wild bovid relatives, cattle have been selectively bred for thousands of years, resulting in much more varied sizes, colors, and temperaments than their wild cousins.
